extracted.intended_audience: science journalists and editors who cover research and journal publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for science reporters working with embargoed journal papers: how to use embargoes productively, add context between embargoes, and navigate journal policies (like the Ingelfinger Rule) to produce deeper, less superficial coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embargo time to study and vet findings
rubrics_metrics.description: “Embargoes give reporters time to study new research and seek out commentary from authoritative voices” — use the embargo period to process and evaluate findings before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend embargo lead time researching background, consulting authoritative commentators, and assessing whether the initial claims are warranted; treat the embargo as an opportunity to vet results rather than merely a countdown to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect embargoes to preserve access
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters who break embargoes risk losing access to information about new findings, emerging technologies, and exciting discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to embargo agreements helps maintain future access to prepublication material and sources; breaking embargoes can lead journals and PR sources to withhold future prepublication access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial, same-moment 'stampede' reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: As John Rennie argues, embargoes encourage superficial and premature reporting: 'Out of fear of being scooped... publish[ing] stories on the same research papers at the moment the embargo ends. In that stampede of coverage, opportunities for distinctive reporting are few.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not race to publish at the instant an embargo lifts just to match competitors; prioritize distinctive reporting and avoid the herd mentality that produces thin, undifferentiated stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce contextual coverage between embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should 'shoot the gaps with coverage that offers nuance and a broadened perspective from which to judge the significance of new findings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create features, explainers, trend pieces, and other reporting in the periods between embargo-driven news cycles to give readers broader perspective and reduce dependence on single-paper coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build annotated timelines of a field's discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Ed Yong crafted a timeline to document the field’s major stories — assembling articles from major journals and coverage into an annotated history to 'look at the stories that lead up to new discoveries, rather than focusing on every new paper in isolation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timelines or similar visualizations (e.g., Dipity) to gather prior papers, coverage, and milestones; these serve both as audience explainers and reporter resources for judging significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create explainer pages and background pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'explainer pages' and 'building background into stories' to provide context applicable across beats and topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare evergreen explainers and backgrounders that can be linked to or updated when new studies appear, so readers understand methods, limits, and the broader research landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report on the practice of science, not only published results
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to report on the practice of science as well as published results — covering processes, incentives, and how research is done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reporting on methodology, peer-review, funding, labs, and cultural practices in science to help readers evaluate findings and understand scientific context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and navigate the Ingelfinger Rule and journal policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals observe the Ingelfinger Rule, 'refusing to publish research that has been reported or commented on elsewhere,' formulated to keep untested findings out of the public sphere but also protecting journal control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of journals' prepublication restrictions, the rationale behind them, and their practical effects; factor these policies into sourcing and publication strategies to avoid unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek ways to report outside journals' restrictions; move upstream
rubrics_metrics.description: Ivan Oransky argues for moving science reporting upstream to cover science before it’s in journals, and for finding ways to do science reporting outside the restrictions imposed by journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preprints, scientists' blogs, conferences, and direct communication with researchers to report on emerging work earlier and diversify story sources beyond formal journal publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage web-based publishing tools and information-visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Yong’s combination of web-based publishing tools and knowledgeable reporting (e.g., Dipity timeline) is presented as a scalable node for adding context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt online tools (timelines, data visualizations, interactive explainers) to create scalable, reusable resources that contextualize new findings for readers and reporters alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical of journals' power and the 'chilling effect' on communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes and the Ingelfinger Rule can exercise a 'chilling effect on communication between scientists — many publicly funded — and journalists,' frustrating attempts to communicate science earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on how journals' commercial and gatekeeping incentives shape coverage; consider advocating for practices that improve access and transparency when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on journals' peer-review filter
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'journals serve a purpose' by applying the imperfect but valuable filter of peer review, the piece suggests reducing heavy reliance on journals as the sole source of vetted science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check journal articles with other sources, expert commentary, replication evidence, and methodological scrutiny rather than assuming journal publication alone equals definitive validation.
